WhatsApp is a free app for sending messages, voice notes, photos, documents and for making voice and video calls over the internet. It uses your **data bundle or Wi-Fi**, not your call credit, so a call to your sister in London costs you only the data it uses. Your account is tied to **one phone number**. The number becomes your WhatsApp identity, so choose a line you plan to keep for years.

There are two official apps, both free. **WhatsApp Messenger** (usually just called WhatsApp) is for personal use. **WhatsApp Business** is a separate app made for small businesses. It adds a business profile, a catalogue, automatic greeting and away messages, quick replies and labels. You can run both on the same phone if you use **two different numbers**, for example your personal MTN line in one and your business Airtel line in the other.

Getting the genuine app

Only install WhatsApp from the **Google Play Store** on Android phones or the **App Store** on iPhones. Search for WhatsApp, and check that the developer is listed as **WhatsApp LLC**. Never install versions passed around as files on WhatsApp or Telegram, such as "GB WhatsApp" or other modified copies. They are not made by WhatsApp, they can steal your messages, and WhatsApp can ban accounts that use them.
Modified WhatsApp apps are a trap

Apps that promise extra features like hiding blue ticks or seeing deleted messages are unofficial. They put your chats, photos and bank details at risk. If you have one, back up what you need, uninstall it and install the official app.
Verifying your number
Open the app and agree to the terms of service.
Select Nigeria (+234) as your country and type your number without the first zero, for example 803 123 4567.
Wait for an SMS with a **six-digit verification code**. Many Android phones read it automatically. If the SMS does not come, choose the option to get the code by phone call.
Type in your **profile name**. This is the name people see when you message them if they have not saved your number. Use your real name or business name, not a nickname like "Sweet Mummy".
Add a clear **profile photo**, then allow WhatsApp to find your contacts if you want your saved contacts to appear.
Your code is like your ATM PIN

The six-digit code proves the number is yours. WhatsApp will never call or message you to ask for it. Anyone who gets your code can take over your account and message your contacts asking for money. Never share it, even with a friend who says the code was sent to you by mistake.
Backing up so you never lose your chats

Your messages live on your phone, not on WhatsApp's servers. If the phone is stolen or spoilt and you have no backup, the chats are gone. On Android, go to **Settings, Chats, Chat backup** and link your **Google account** (Google Drive). On iPhone, the backup goes to **iCloud**. Set the backup frequency to daily or weekly, and choose whether to include videos, because videos make the backup large and use more data. Many people choose to back up only on Wi-Fi to save their bundle.
Worked example: moving WhatsApp to a new phone
For example, Bisi in Ibadan buys a new Android phone and wants her customers' chats on it. Her old phone still works.
On the old phone she opens Settings, Chats, Chat backup and taps Back up, while connected to Wi-Fi.
She checks the screen shows the backup time as just now, linked to her Google account.
She inserts her SIM in the new phone, installs WhatsApp from the Play Store and signs in to the same Google account.
She verifies her number with the six-digit SMS code.
WhatsApp finds the backup and offers to Restore. She taps Restore and waits while the chats load, then the media.
All her chats and voice notes appear on the new phone. She now leaves daily backup switched on.

If your old phone is lost, you can still restore from Google Drive or iCloud on the new phone, as long as you had backups switched on before the loss. First get a replacement SIM with the same number from your network's office, then install WhatsApp and verify. Verifying on a new phone also logs the old phone out of WhatsApp, which protects you if a thief has it.
Keep the app updated

WhatsApp regularly fixes security problems and adds features. Open the Play Store or App Store every few weeks, search WhatsApp and tap **Update** if you see it, or switch on automatic updates. Two-step verification: the most important setting

Two-step verification adds a **six-digit PIN that you create**. After it is on, anyone trying to register your number on a new phone needs both the SMS code and your PIN. Even if a fraudster tricks you or your network into giving away the SMS code, they still cannot get in without the PIN.

The PIN is a second lock that the SMS code alone cannot open.
Open Settings, then Account, then Two-step verification.
Tap Turn on (or Create PIN) and type a six-digit PIN you will remember. Do not use your birthday, 123456 or your ATM PIN.
Type it again to confirm.
Add an **email address** you can open. WhatsApp uses it to send you a reset link if you forget the PIN. You can skip it, but it is wiser to add it.
Write the PIN somewhere safe at home, not in your phone notes.

WhatsApp will sometimes ask you to enter the PIN while you use the app. This is normal: it helps you remember it. Never type your PIN into a link someone sends you, and never read it to anyone on the phone.
Worked example: a near miss

For example, Chioma in Owerri sells hair products. One evening she gets a message from her cousin's account: "I mistakenly sent my code to your number, please send it to me." At the same time an SMS with a six-digit code arrives.
She recognises the pattern: someone is trying to register HER number on another phone. Her cousin's account has probably already been hijacked.
She does not send the code and calls her cousin on a normal phone call. The cousin says she did not send the message.
Chioma opens Settings, Account, Two-step verification and turns it on with a new PIN and her email.
She warns her cousin to recover her account by verifying her number again and to report the problem to WhatsApp support from Settings, Help.
Chioma's account stays safe. With two-step verification on, the fraudster would need her PIN even if she had slipped and shared the code.
More locks you can use
**App lock:** use your fingerprint, face or phone passcode to open WhatsApp (in Privacy settings on Android, or Screen lock on iPhone).
**Chat lock:** lock one sensitive chat behind your fingerprint or passcode, so it is hidden from anyone who borrows your phone.
**Disappearing messages:** set new messages in a chat to vanish after 24 hours, 7 days or 90 days. Useful for private matters, but remember people can still screenshot.
**Blocked contacts:** a list of people you have blocked. They cannot call or message you.

Deciding what to do with a chat

Four quick actions keep your most important conversations at the top.
**Pin:** press and hold a chat, then tap the pin icon. You can pin up to three chats to the top, for example your husband, your main supplier and your business group.
**Mute:** press and hold, tap the mute (speaker) icon and choose 8 hours, 1 week or Always. You still get messages, but your phone stays quiet.
**Archive:** press and hold, then tap the archive box. The chat moves to the Archived folder at the top of your list. It is not deleted and you can open it any time.
**Mark as unread:** press and hold, then Mark as unread, to remind yourself to reply later.
Worked example: cleaning up 300 chats
For example, Halima runs a small kitchen in Kaduna selling meals to offices. Her chat list has over 300 chats, and she keeps missing orders.
She pins her three busiest office customers so they stay at the top.
She mutes six family and alumni groups for Always and checks them in the evening.
She archives 150 old chats from last year's customers. They are still saved, just out of the way.
She renames 40 customer contacts using her pattern, for example "Musa Office Barnawa".
Now when she opens WhatsApp at 11am, the first five chats are the people most likely to order lunch, and she stops missing orders.
Blocking and reporting

If someone harasses you, sends you suspicious links or tries to scam you, open their chat, tap their name or number at the top, scroll down and tap **Block**. A blocked contact cannot message you, call you or see your updates. You can also tap **Report**. Reporting sends WhatsApp the most recent messages from that person so they can investigate the account. Blocking does not tell the person you blocked them, but they may notice that their messages show only one tick.
Unknown number messaging you?

When an unsaved number messages you for the first time, WhatsApp shows options to Block or Add to contacts, and often shows whether you share any groups. Read the first message carefully before replying, and do not open links from strangers.
Deleting a contact

To delete a contact, you remove it from your phone's contact list (or open the contact in WhatsApp and choose Edit, then Delete). The chat history stays until you delete the chat itself. Deleting a contact does not block them: they can still message you, and the chat will just show their number instead of a name.
Contacts on a shared or family phone

Use **App lock** or **Chat lock** for business chats so customers' details stay private. Then a new phone brings back both your chats, from the WhatsApp backup, and the names, from your Google or iCloud contacts.

Clock: not yet sent

Ticks show how far your message has travelled, from your phone to being read.

A **clock** means the message has not left your phone, usually because you have no data or network. **One grey tick** means it reached WhatsApp but not the other phone, perhaps because it is off or offline, or because the person has blocked you. **Two grey ticks** mean it was delivered to their phone. **Two blue ticks** mean they opened the chat. In a group, ticks turn blue only when everyone has read it. Press and hold your message and tap **Info** to see exactly who read it and when. Remember: if someone has switched off read receipts, you will never see blue ticks from them.
Inside a chat
**Top bar:** the contact's name and photo. Tap it to see their info, shared media, and options like mute, disappearing messages and block. The phone and camera icons start calls.
**Typing box:** type a message, tap the emoji face for emojis, the paperclip or plus for files, photos, location, contact and polls, and the camera for a quick photo.
**Microphone:** hold to record a voice message. It turns into a send arrow once you type text.
**Search:** inside a chat, use Search to find an old message by a word, such as "address" or "account number".
Saving data with Storage and data

In Settings, **Storage and data** has three useful parts. **Manage storage** shows which chats take up the most space and lets you delete large videos you no longer need. **Media auto-download** lets you choose which files download by themselves on mobile data, on Wi-Fi or when roaming. **Use less data for calls** reduces the data voice and video calls use.
Worked example: stopping videos from eating your bundle
For example, Grace in Benin City buys a 1.5GB monthly bundle for about 1,000 naira (approximate, prices change). It finishes in ten days because of videos from her church and family groups.
She opens Settings, Storage and data, Media auto-download.
Under When using mobile data, she ticks only Photos and unticks Audio, Videos and Documents.
Under When connected on Wi-Fi, she leaves everything ticked for when she is at the office.
In Manage storage she deletes 2GB of old forwarded videos and frees space on her phone.
Videos now show a download button and only download when she taps them. Her bundle lasts much longer.
WhatsApp on a laptop

If you type a lot, use WhatsApp on a computer. Open **web.whatsapp.com** in a browser or install the WhatsApp desktop app from the official site or app store. On your phone, open Settings (or the three dots), tap **Linked devices**, then **Link a device**, and scan the QR code on the computer screen. Your chats appear on the laptop. You can link up to four devices to one WhatsApp account, and they keep working for a while even if your phone goes offline.
Check your linked devices

Open Linked devices from time to time. If you see a computer or browser you do not recognise, tap it and choose Log out. Someone who briefly had your phone could have linked their laptop to read your messages.

Editing and deleting
**Edit:** press and hold a message you sent and tap Edit. You can edit for up to 15 minutes after sending. The message then shows the word "Edited".

If you cannot tick every box, do not forward the message.

Messages you forward show a small **Forwarded** label. If a message has been forwarded through a chain of five or more chats, it shows **Forwarded many times** with a double arrow, and WhatsApp limits it so it can only be forwarded to one chat at a time. That label is a warning sign: viral messages about free government grants, miracle cures, kidnapping alerts or bank closures are very often false. Check trusted news sources or official websites, such as a ministry's or bank's own page, before sharing.
Fake grant and recruitment messages

Messages offering free money, scholarships or jobs that ask you to click a link, fill in your BVN or bank details, or forward to ten groups are scams. Real programmes do not ask you to forward them to unlock a reward.
Polite, professional wording

Text has no tone of voice, so short messages can sound rude by accident. "Ok" or "Send money" may feel cold to the person reading. Start with a greeting, use the person's name, and end with a clear next step: "Good morning Mrs Bello. Your order is ready. Would you like delivery today or tomorrow?" Avoid writing whole sentences in capital letters, which reads as shouting, and avoid long chains of emojis in business chats. If a message upsets you, wait a few minutes before replying, or call instead. A calm reply protects relationships with customers, colleagues and family.

She pins the poll and mentions the five executive members with @ to vote first.

Two-step verification adds a six-digit PIN that you create. Then anyone trying to register your number on a new phone needs the SMS code and your PIN.
Step one. Open Settings, then Account, then Two-step verification.
Step two. Tap Turn on and type a six-digit PIN you will remember. Do not use your birthday, 123456, or your ATM PIN.
Step three. Type it again to confirm.
Step four. Add an email address you can open. WhatsApp uses it to send you a reset link if you forget the PIN.
Step five. Write the PIN somewhere safe at home, not in your phone notes.

Which tool does which job?

A group is for conversation. Everyone sees and replies to every message. It can hold up to 1,024 members, good for teams, cooperatives and church departments.

A community links related groups, like branches, with one announcement group that reaches every member.
